dimension.title: Individual
dimension.description: Individual progression is defined by individual choice and the individual impact of the progression. In-game activities can vary from individual to fully cooperative but progression affects the individual.

dimensionExamples.example: In this game the player only has control over himself.

dimension.title: Single
dimension.description: Single applies to any game where players have control of one single entity.

dimensionExamples.example: In this game, the player cannot change the characteristics of the car, only the pod can choose it. cars are not the same, they have certain differences such as, for example, their "hitbox".

dimension.title: Pool
dimension.description: Pool describes when players are given an array of playable entities to choose from (e.g. characters, nations, class). These have predefined gameplay characteristics and in some cases, players can be forced to have a unique selection.

dimensionExamples.example: There's no changes in the car of the player.

dimension.title: Static
dimension.description: When the player's entity is constant throughout gameplay.

dimensionExamples.example: In this game, jodars are unique individuals who end up competing against each other in different game sessions.

dimension.title: Competitors
dimension.description: Competitors, where you may be able to compete with other players, either momentarily or through the whole game session (e.g. team vs team match-based games).

dimensionExamples.example: All players have the same vision of the game.

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared world views apply to a game when players have access to the same world.

dimension.title: Distinct
dimension.description: Distinct refers to when each player has control of their own individual viewpoint, typically through separate screens.

dimensionExamples.example: Each person can perform like they want to.

dimension.title: Free Collaboration
dimension.description: In free collaboration, players can take on available tasks as they wish and decide how to contribute.

dimensionExamples.example: There is simultaneous collaboration, as a team, in search of victory.

dimension.title: Concurrent Collaboration
dimension.description: In concurrent collaboration, players have to perform gameplay tasks concurrently.

dimensionExamples.example:
Communication is not mandatory, but it can happen. 
The player communicates if he wants, according to his desire.

dimension.title: Agnostic
dimension.description: When Agnostic, the game is neutral to player communication, it does not incentivise nor it places any restrictions. It is the only communication design that does not promote cooperation.

dimension.title: Limited
dimension.description: When Limited, the game restricts communication, while not prohibiting it as a whole. It can be achieved through gameplay mechanics such as designated time/space when communication is allowed, or through allowing communication through only specific modalities only (e.g. pings, emotes); or through rules that the players should follow (e.g. do not communicate your exact position).

dimension.title: Text Chat
dimension.description: Support for players to communicate using text

dimension.title: Premade Messages
dimension.description: Players can communicate through specific messages, previously created (possibly by the developers)

dimension.title: Voice Chat
dimension.description: Support for players to communicate using their voice

dimension.title: Emotes
dimension.description: Players can communicate through particular animations their characters have (e.g. pointing at something)

dimension.title: Task
dimension.description: Task refers to gameplay tasks where at least one player is dependent on another. These can force players to coordinate to be effective and complete them.

dimension.title: Grouping
dimension.description: Grouping refers to activities that require a certain number of players to be accessed/completed.

dimension.title: Assistive Actions
dimension.description: Assistive Actions encompass actions that one player performs to the benefit of other/s (i.e. note that the player can have indirect benefits such as reviving others to increase their own chances of success). In these games, players can support and assist other players in achieving their objectives.

dimension.title: Consumables
dimension.description: Consumables refer to items that exist in a limited amount and can be utilised by players to invoke an effect (usually existing as a form of currency, materials, or food) or are not consumed on purpose by players but support the gameplay (e.g., health, energy). Consumables are shared when the agency to consume and manage them pertains to more than one player.

dimension.title: Usefulness
dimension.description: Usefulness happens when a certain resource or information (shared among multiple players) is more valuable  to one of those players. It can promote collaboration and coordination to maximise player performance/enjoyment.

dimension.title: Synergies
dimension.description: Synergies extended from Rocha et. al 2008 allow one entity to assist or change the game actions (e.g. abilities) of another.

dimensionExamples.example: The cooperative formation of groups in this game is done when a match starts, bringing together several online players in each team.

dimension.title: Organised Grouping
dimension.description: Organised Grouping covers all features that establish groups/communities (e.g. guilds) within games, which typically persist across different gaming sessions and may have defined roles and/or hierarchy.

dimensionExamples.example: Here the objectives work as a team, there are unique actions that each player can do to achieve objectives, but there is the main objective of winning the game as a team, scoring goals.

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared goals consist of singular objectives that multiple players pursue and work together to achieve
